title: Racing Abroad in Southeast Asia: Your First Trip
seo_title: Racing Abroad in Southeast Asia: Your First Race Trip
meta_description: Entry fees, foreigner rates, Thailand's new 30-day visa rule, arrival cards, race-pack collection and what to pack: a practical guide to your first race trip in Southeast Asia.
dek: Racing in another Southeast Asian country is easier than racing almost anywhere else: short flights, generous visa rules and races in nearly every month. What catches first-timers out is the logistics around the race, from foreigner entry rates and arrival cards to race packs that can only be collected the day before.

sections.heading: Choose a race that works as a trip
paragraphs: Some races make better trip anchors than others. A race in a walkable city with plenty to see, such as Chiang Mai, Hoi An, Siem Reap or Luang Prabang, turns easily into a few days away. A flagship city marathon brings a bigger expo, more aid stations and more road closures; a smaller regional race is simpler to get around but has less built for visitors. If anyone in your group isn't running the full distance, look at the shorter races: 376 of the 446 races in the Run SEA calendar (84%) offer a 5K or shorter, and 100 (22%) offer 3K or less, which often suits children[1].

Entry fees are low by international standards. Of the races in our calendar that include a full marathon and publish fees, the top of each race's price range, usually the marathon, runs from about RM90 to RM270 in Malaysia, PHP 1,499 to 3,499 in the Philippines, THB 700 to 2,500 in Thailand, VND 800,000 to 2,000,000 in Vietnam and IDR 550,000 to about 1.8 million in Indonesia; Singapore's marathon tops out at S$208[1]. A fuller comparison is at runsea.run/articles/what-race-weekend-actually-costs-southeast-asia/.

Some races charge foreigners more or limit what they can enter. The Phnom Penh International Half Marathon charged US$28 for Cambodians and US$45 for foreign runners in 2026, the Sanur Bali International Half Marathon charges foreign runners IDR 1,490,000 for 2027, and the Maybank Marathon in Bali enters runners by ballot with higher fees for foreigners[1]. A few races are closed to visitors altogether: Malioboro Run in Yogyakarta was open only to Indonesian citizens in 2026, and Malaysia's Merdeka Half Marathon and Pahang Marathon take only residents. Others let you run but not win: at the MILO Marathon national finals and some Indonesian races, podium places and prize money go only to citizens or residents[1].

sections.heading: Visas and arrival cards
paragraphs: Citizens of ASEAN countries have the easiest time. The ASEAN Framework Agreement on Visa Exemption sets a baseline of up to 14 days visa-free for citizens of other member states visiting with a valid national passport, put into effect through agreements between pairs of member states[2].

Thailand changed its rules on 15 September 2026. Its 60-day visa exemption ended, and the foreign ministry's new list gives citizens of 60 countries and territories, including Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Brunei, the UK, the US, Australia and Japan, visa-free entry for tourism of up to 30 days[3][4]. The new exemption covers tourism only. Visa-exempt travellers entering Thailand by land are limited to two entries a calendar year, but Malaysian, Singaporean, Indonesian and Bruneian citizens are exempt from that cap, which matters for runners driving to races in southern Thailand[4].

Indonesia gives citizens of ASEAN countries, including Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines, Thailand, Brunei and Vietnam, a visa exemption of up to 30 days with no fee, which cannot be extended[9]. Visitors from countries such as the UK, US, Australia and Japan need a visa on arrival instead: Rp500,000 for 30 days, extendable once for another 30, and available online in advance as an e-VOA[9][10]. Either way, bring a passport valid for at least six months and an onward ticket[9].

Vietnam's visa-free stay depends on the passport. Singapore passport holders can generally stay up to 30 days per entry[13], and Vietnam's national tourism authority lists 30 days for Malaysians and Thais, 21 days for Filipinos, and 45 days for citizens of 25 mostly European countries, including the UK, Germany, France, Japan and South Korea[14]. Other visitors, including Americans and Australians, need a visa: the e-visa from the official portal evisa.gov.vn is valid for up to 90 days, single or multiple entry, and costs US$25 or US$50[15]. For any other passport, including Indonesian and Bruneian, check the official site, evisa.gov.vn, before booking[15].

Visa-free doesn't mean no paperwork. Thailand requires every non-Thai visitor to submit the Thailand Digital Arrival Card online, free, within three days before arrival[5]. Singapore requires the SG Arrival Card from all travellers except residents crossing at the land checkpoints, also free and within three days before arrival, counting the arrival day[6]. Malaysia runs its own Malaysia Digital Arrival Card, and the Philippines its free eTravel registration[7][8]. Indonesia requires every arriving passenger to complete the All Indonesia arrival card, which combines the immigration, customs, health and quarantine declarations, is free, and can be submitted within three days before arrival[10][11][12]. Vietnam's online pre-arrival declaration is so far compulsory only for foreigners flying into Tan Son Nhat airport in Ho Chi Minh City, but the Immigration Department recommends it for all visitors, at prearrival.immigration.gov.vn[13][15]. Use only the government portals, since agent sites charge for forms that are free, and check the rules for your own passport on the destination government's site before you book anything you can't refund.

sections.heading: Race packs: collect them before race day
paragraphs: Assume you cannot collect your bib on race morning. Among the race records in our calendar that describe pack collection, at least 15 state outright that there is no race-day collection, and almost all the rest hold it in the days before the race, usually the last one to three[1]. The only exception we found was the Yoma Yangon International Marathon, which let overseas runners collect on race morning in 2026. Two races post kits instead of handing them out: the Great Eastern Women's Run couriered packs to Singapore addresses, and the Pos Malaysia Run posts kits to your home[1].

Collection can be a long way from the start. Three races near BSD City, outside Jakarta, hand out packs in central Jakarta, the UI Half Marathon collects at Kemang Village in South Jakarta for a race in Depok, and Garmin Run Singapore's collection is at Science Park, about 9 km from the start[1]. Windows can be short: the Northernmost race at Padang Besar collects only on the Friday afternoon from 3pm to 7pm, and for the 2025 Garmin Run in Putrajaya, packs were collected in Petaling Jaya two weeks before race day[1].

Bring photo ID that matches your registration. Songkhla Marathon requires passports from foreign runners at collection, two Thai races check runners with Face ID, and some races let someone collect for you with your authorisation while others insist on the runner in person[1]. Go early in the collection window: queues are worst in the final hours, and Putrajaya's 2025 collection saw two-hour waits[1]. Keep the expo to an hour, and save any new shoes or gear bought there for a later race.

sections.heading: Time the trip around a pre-dawn start
paragraphs: Most of the region's big races start well before sunrise, so arrival day matters more than it seems (see runsea.run/articles/why-southeast-asia-races-start-before-dawn/). Arrive two or three days ahead if you can. That gives you time to collect the pack without rushing, do one short shakeout run at your race-morning wake-up time, and check how you will get to the start before public transport is running. Road closures can make a hotel that looks close to the start hard to leave by car on race morning, so check the closure map against your route.

Keep sightseeing for after the race. Long walking days and unfamiliar food in the two days before a race cost more than most travellers expect, and the day after a marathon is a bad time for a hike. Plan one easy day after the race, then do the demanding things. If you want to fit two races into one trip, leave several recovery days between them, more in the heat.

sections.heading: If family or friends are coming
paragraphs: For supporters, race day can be longer and hotter than it is for the runner: an early start, a long wait and no moving air. Pick one or two viewing points you can actually reach given the road closures, and agree a meeting point after the finish in case phones die. Supporters with young children are often better off arriving near your expected finish time rather than at the start. Shade, water, sunscreen and a folding stool make a long wait easier, and a sign with your name or bib number helps you spot each other in a crowd.
Check whether the race has a children's category, what the finish area offers and whether a stroller is practical near the start and finish, and confirm these with the organiser before you travel.

sections.heading: What to pack
paragraphs: Lay out race-morning kit first, before anything else: shoes, race clothes, watch, gels or drink mix you have trained with, a running belt for phone and essentials, and the registration confirmation and ID for collection. Carry that kit in your cabin bag so a delayed suitcase can't cost you the race. Add a charged power bank, since your phone is your ticket, map and ride home on race morning, and a universal plug adapter, because socket types vary across the region. For clothing and what to carry during the race itself, see runsea.run/articles/what-to-wear-and-carry-tropical-race/.

If you'd rather someone else handled entry, transfers and pack collection, especially for ballot races or races far from an airport, a race-travel package can help; runsea.run/articles/using-a-race-travel-agency-when-a-package-is-worth-it/ explains when one is worth paying for.

faqs.question: Do I need a visa to race in Southeast Asia?
faqs.answer: Often not, but it depends on your passport and destination. ASEAN citizens get at least 14 days visa-free in other member states. Since 15 September 2026, Thailand gives visitors from 60 countries and territories, including the UK, US, Australia and five ASEAN members, up to 30 days visa-free for tourism. Check the destination government's own site before booking.

faqs.question: Can I collect my race pack on race morning?
faqs.answer: Usually not. In the Run SEA calendar, at least 15 races state outright that there is no race-day collection, and most others hold it in the last few days before the race, sometimes far from the start. Plan to arrive in time for the collection window and bring photo ID matching your registration.

faqs.question: Do foreign runners pay more to enter Southeast Asian races?
faqs.answer: At some races, yes. The Phnom Penh International Half Marathon charged US$28 for Cambodians and US$45 for foreigners in 2026, and Bali's Maybank Marathon charges foreigners more. A few races are open only to citizens or residents, and some restrict prize money to locals, so read the entry rules before you book travel.

editorial_notes: Rewritten 6 Nov 2026 as the site's single first-trip travel guide, absorbing the race-cation, family-trip, visa-free, race-expo, packing-checklist and spectator-gear pieces. Fee ranges are the top of each published range for races with a full marathon in Run SEA's entity records (some are late-registration prices). Pack-collection facts come from the race records, which cite organiser pages; '15 races' counts records stating there is no race-day collection. Visa and arrival-card rules were checked on official government pages on 2026-11-06: the Thai MFA 30-day list is dated 15 Sep 2026 and the ICA page was updated 28 Oct 2026; the end of Thailand's 60-day scheme and the land-entry cap are from TTG Asia's report on the Royal Gazette notices. Indonesia's and Vietnam's rules were added on 2026-11-06. Indonesia: A1 visa-exemption and B1 visa-on-arrival terms were read in the evisa.imigrasi.go.id visa-selection tool (tourism purpose) for Malaysian, Singaporean, Philippine, Thai, Vietnamese and Bruneian passports (A1 offered) and Australian, US, UK and Japanese passports (B1 only); the three-day arrival-card notice is on the e-Visa home page; All Indonesia's nationwide scope and merged declarations are from the immigration directorate's 1 Oct 2025 press release, and its free status from the Batam immigration office's Sep 2025 notice. Vietnam: e-visa length and fees and the pre-arrival recommendation are from evisa.gov.vn; the Singapore 30-day stay and the Tan Son Nhat-only pre-arrival requirement are from Singapore MFA's Vietnam page (updated 6 Nov 2026); other visa-free periods are from the Vietnam National Authority of Tourism page marked 2026. Vietnam's stays for Indonesian, Bruneian and other ASEAN passports are deliberately not given: the tourism authority lists Indonesia at 14 days, which other reports contradict (30 days), and the Immigration Department's own exemption list, linked from evisa.gov.vn through a t.ly short link, could not be opened.
